items.title: The earliest Christians thought Jesus would return within their lifetime
items.claim: Paul's letters (50s CE) are the oldest Christian texts. What does he tell his churches about the timing of Christ's return?

options.text: He explicitly warns that it will be many centuries away
He tells believers — in 1 Thessalonians 4 and 1 Corinthians 15 — that 'we who are alive, who are left' will be caught up to meet the Lord
He refuses to discuss the timing at all
He places the return precisely at AD 70, the destruction of the Temple

items.reveal:
1 Thessalonians 4:15-17, written around 50-51 CE, includes Paul among those still alive at the Parousia. 1 Corinthians 7:29 says 'the appointed time has grown short.' Mark 9:1 has Jesus saying 'some standing here will not taste death' before seeing the Kingdom.

When Christ did not return, later texts (e.g. 2 Peter 3:8 — 'one day is with the Lord as a thousand years') reinterpret the delay. This shift is one of the central transformations of early Christian theology.
items.why: Treating the New Testament as a unified, settled doctrine misses that it documents a community reinterpreting itself in real time. The 'delay of the Parousia' is one of the formative pressures on Christian thought.

items.title: The Five Pillars have a canonical order — beginning with Shahada
items.claim: What is the standard Sunni order of the Five Pillars of Islam?

options.text: Shahada (declaration of faith), Salah (five daily prayers), Zakat (almsgiving, 2.5% of accumulated wealth), Sawm (fasting in Ramadan), Hajj (pilgrimage to Mecca, once if able)

items.reveal:
The Hadith of Gabriel (recorded in Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim) lists the Pillars in this order. The Shahada is the doorway — 'There is no god but God, and Muhammad is the messenger of God'.

Shia Islam (Twelver tradition) frames obligations differently. They recognise the practices but as part of the Furu al-Din (Ten Ancillaries of the Religion), alongside jihad, enjoining good and forbidding wrong, tawalla (love of the household of the Prophet) and tabarra (disassociation from enemies).

Zakat is calculated annually on accumulated wealth above a threshold (nisab); Sawm requires no food, drink or marital relations from dawn (fajr) to sunset (maghrib) during Ramadan.
items.why: Religious practice has specific structure. Treating the Pillars as a vague list of good acts misses the theological logic — faith first, then prayer, then social action.

items.title: Kant gave multiple formulations of the categorical imperative
items.claim: How does Kant's categorical imperative work?

options.text: A single rule: do unto others as you would have them do to you

Multiple formulations including universalisability ('act only according to that maxim by which you can at the same time will that it should become a universal law') and humanity-as-end ('act so as to treat humanity, in your own person or another's, always as an end, never as a means only')
An empirical rule derived from observation

items.reveal:
Kant's 'Groundwork of the Metaphysics of Morals' (1785) sets out the categorical imperative. Standard count: three formulations.

Formula of Universal Law: 'Act only according to that maxim by which you can at the same time will that it should become a universal law.'
Formula of Humanity: 'Act so as to treat humanity... always as an end, never as a means only.'
Formula of the Kingdom of Ends: 'Act according to the maxims of a member of a merely possible kingdom of ends.'

Kant's most famous example — lying to the murderer at the door — shows the strict reading: lying is universally impermissible.
items.why: Kantian ethics is sometimes reduced to 'don't lie'. The multiple formulations and the humanity-as-end principle are richer — and more humane — than the slogan suggests.
